1 Recovery phrase

Generate a fresh phrase or type an existing one. The last word carries a checksum, so a phrase invented by hand will almost never validate.

Words
Entropy

The raw randomness behind the phrase. Generate fills this with the bytes it drew; you can also type your own from dice, coins or cards and the phrase is rebuilt from it. The checksum is added for you. Dice are hashed exactly as typed, the way hardware wallets that accept dice do it, with the word count taken from the Words selector: 50 rolls are enough for 12 words, 100 for 24. Other inputs are used raw unless you choose a word count.

Advanced feature. Entropy must come from something genuinely random: fair dice, fair coins, a well-shuffled deck. Not song lyrics, not key-mashing, not your birthday. You are not a good source of entropy, and a phrase built from weak entropy can be guessed.

Raw mode does not match hardware wallets. You chose "Raw entropy" with dice. Pick a word count in the Mnemonic length menu to hash the rolls the way wallets that accept dice do.

The phrase will look more secure than it really is. A fixed length was chosen with fewer real bits than it needs, so the missing bits are made up by hashing. Only the real bits protect you.

    2 Shamir backup SLIP-39

    Split the entropy behind the phrase into SLIP-39 shares, the Shamir standard used by Trezor. Choose how many shares to make and how many are needed to recover; any set that meets the threshold rebuilds the exact phrase above, while fewer shares reveal nothing at all.

    Write every share down now. Each click of Create shares makes a brand-new set with its own identifier, and shares from different sets cannot be combined. To confirm the backup works, switch to Recover and paste in a threshold of them.

    Loading these shares straight into a Trezor as a Shamir wallet would create a different wallet, because Trezor turns the recovered secret into keys its own way. Always recover through this tool (or any SLIP-39 tool) to get the BIP39 phrase back, then use the phrase.

    Paste enough shares above.

    3 Seed & master key

    The phrase and passphrase are stretched into a 512-bit seed, and the seed becomes the BIP32 master key at the root of the tree.

    Master fingerprint—The first four bytes of the master key's hash. Wallets show it so you can confirm a phrase and passphrase are the ones you expect, without revealing anything.
    Waiting for a valid phrase…
    BIP85: derive a new phrase from this master key

    BIP85 turns one master phrase into any number of independent child phrases, one per index. Back up only the master; every child can be recreated from it. The result is not used anywhere else on this page. To use a derived phrase, paste it into the phrase field above.

    Needs a private root key.

    Your multisig xpub

    This is what you hand to the person setting up the multisig wallet: your master fingerprint, the path, and the public account key. It cannot spend anything. Share it; never share the private one.

    Taproot multisig (script type 3') is the newest type, with cheaper and more private spends. Sparrow, Bitcoin Core 24 and later, and recent hardware wallets support it; older wallets cannot import it, and there is no special prefix for its key: it is a plain xpub.

    6 Multisig wallet

    A multisig wallet is controlled by several seeds and needs some of them, for example 2 of 3, to spend. Each seed is one recovery phrase, kept on its own device. KeyPath combines their public keys (xpubs) into the wallet; it never needs the seeds. Pick what you are doing:

    Paste the xpub from each device, or an existing wallet's xpubs or setup file, and choose how many signatures are needed.

    KeyPath creates every seed here and builds the wallet from their xpubs. This is the simplest way, but every seed passes through this computer. For the strongest setup, create each seed on its own device and use Build a wallet from xpubs.

    How a multisig wallet is set up
    1 · Seeds

    Make each seed on its own device, ideally a hardware wallet, one per person. Nobody ever sees anyone else's seed.

    2 · Export

    Each device exports the public xpub of its seed, as one line with the fingerprint and path (the BIP48 tab above shows it for the seed on this page). Xpubs are safe to send by email or chat.

    3 · Combine

    Whoever sets up the wallet pastes every xpub line below, picks how many signatures are needed, and gets the wallet definition: the descriptor for Sparrow, Bitcoin Core or Nunchuk, and the setup file for each hardware wallet. Both are public and contain no seed; each device keeps its own seed and learns from the file which wallet it belongs to.

    4 · Verify

    Every device should show the first receive address listed here for the wallet. If one device disagrees, stop: an xpub, the threshold or the script type is wrong.

    5 · Back up

    Keep the descriptor or setup file with every seed backup. Recovering a multisig wallet needs enough seeds to sign and the xpub of every seed, which is what the definition holds. Two seeds of a 2-of-3 can sign, but without the third seed's xpub the addresses cannot even be rebuilt. Prove it with the demo wallet: delete one xpub line and watch the address change.

    of

    Taproot multisig is the newest type: spending is cheaper and reveals less about the wallet. It is supported by Sparrow, Bitcoin Core 24 and later, and recent hardware wallets; older wallets cannot import it. Every device holding a seed must support it.

    Write each seed down and store them apart.

    Your wallet definition

    This is your wallet's definition: its policy, its script type and the xpub of every seed. It is public information; it cannot spend and it contains no seed. KeyPath gives it in two formats, one for software wallets and one for hardware wallets. Back it up with every seed. Without it, even enough seeds to sign cannot find the coins.

    Separate receive and change descriptors

    Some software wants receive and change addresses as two separate lines. The single line above covers both.

    About entropy

    Notes for the entropy panel.

    Show the entropy notes
    Checksum

    Entropy values should not include the BIP39 checksum. It is added automatically.

    Source

    Entropy must come from a strong source of randomness: flipping a fair coin, rolling a fair dice, noise measurements. Not phrases from books, song lyrics, your birthday or street address, or keyboard mashing. Chances are overwhelming it is not random enough.

    Storage

    Do not store entropy. Keeping a deck of cards in a specific shuffled order is unreliable compared to storing the phrase. Store the mnemonic generated from the entropy instead.

    Generate

    The Generate button uses the browser's cryptographically secure random number generator, which can generally be trusted more than your own intuition about randomness.

    Dice

    When dice are detected, KeyPath hashes the rolls exactly as typed (digits 1 to 6) and takes the word count from the Words selector, which is the convention of hardware wallets that accept dice. A wallet that hashes dice the same way will produce the same phrase. Choose "Raw entropy" in the Mnemonic length menu only if you specifically want the unhashed base-6 conversion, which no hardware wallet reproduces.

    Cards

    Card entropy assumes cards are replaced after each draw, not drawn one after another. A full deck with replacement gives 232 bits of entropy (21 words); without replacement, 225 bits.

    Time to crack

    The estimate assumes an attacker who knows your method and tries every possibility at ten billion guesses per second. It reflects the number of bits, not whether your dice were fair.

    Security

    What this file does to protect you, and what only you can do. Short version: work offline, verify the hash, keep secrets off the clipboard and off camera.

    Show the security details
    No network

    One self-contained file with no external scripts, fonts or images. A Content Security Policy baked into the page blocks every outbound connection and refuses to run any script other than the two it was built with, so an injected script cannot run. Nothing you type leaves this page.

    No storage

    Your phrase, seed and keys are never written to disk. The only things remembered between visits are the theme and the tooltip setting. Fields are wiped when you leave the page, and private values are blurred automatically whenever a phrase is generated and again after five minutes without activity.

    Clipboard

    Copying a secret puts it on your system clipboard, which some clipboard managers and phone-to-computer sync features upload. KeyPath clears its copy from the clipboard after 60 seconds. Copy secrets only when you must, and never on a machine that syncs its clipboard.

    Randomness

    Generate uses the browser's cryptographically secure random number generator. Cryptography comes from the audited noble and scure libraries; address derivation, Shamir sharing and Seed QR were checked against the official test vectors of each standard.

    Verify

    Only trust a copy of this file whose SHA-256 hash matches the one published with the release. On a Mac or Linux: shasum -a 256 keypath.html. On Windows PowerShell: Get-FileHash keypath.html. The expected value is in SHA256SUMS.txt next to the download. A page cannot vouch for itself; the hash is how you know it has not been tampered with.

    Your part

    For real funds: save this file, move it to a computer that is disconnected from the internet, and open it in a fresh browser profile with no extensions. Extensions can read every page, including this one. Do not print, screenshot or photograph secrets, and close the tab when you are done. Nothing here protects you from malware already on the computer.

    Take it offline

    Download the file, check its hash, and open it on a computer that is not connected to the internet. The download always comes from the latest GitHub release, saved as keypath.html.
